title: Finite minimal-volume classes and their smooth trait base changes
statement: Let $R$ be a discrete valuation ring with uniformizer $\pi$, fraction field $E$, residue field $k$, and $T=\operatorname{Spec}R$ [def-sc-discrete-valuation-ring, def-weil-affine-spectrum]. Products and fibres are scheme-theoretic base changes [def-pc-base-change]. Smooth and finite type have the meanings of [def-sbc-smooth-morphisms, def-weil-finite-type-morphism]; separated means that the diagonal is a closed immersion [def-weil-closed-immersion]. Write $R^{\mathrm{sh}}$ for a strict henselization at a geometric closed point and $E^{\mathrm{sh}}=\operatorname{Frac}(R^{\mathrm{sh}})$ [def-weil-geometric-point, def-weil-pbc-strict-henselization-limit]. A subset $C\subseteq X(E^{\mathrm{sh}})$ of a finite-type $E$-scheme is bounded if some finite affine cover $U_i=\operatorname{Spec}B_i$, finite $E$-algebra generating lists $b_{ij}$, decomposition $C=\bigcup_i C_i$ with $C_i\subseteq U_i(E^{\mathrm{sh}})$, and integers $c_i$ satisfy $v(b_{ij}(x))\geq c_i$ for $x\in C_i$, where $v(0)=+\infty$. An open in a scheme over a trait is base-dense if it is dense in each fibre. A rational map over that trait is a morphism on a base-dense open, modulo agreement on a base-dense common open; its domain of definition is the union of all representative domains. A birational map over the trait is an isomorphism between base-dense opens. For a smooth separated finite-type $E$-scheme $X$, a smooth model means a smooth separated finite-type $T$-scheme $M$ with a specified identification $M_E\simeq X$. Let $G/E$ be a smooth separated finite-type group scheme of dimension $d$, with group operations as in [def-sc-group-scheme]. Fix a nowhere vanishing left-invariant section $\omega$ of $\Omega^d_{G/E}=\bigwedge^d\Omega^1_{G/E}$ [def-sc-relative-differential-sheaf, def-sc-sheaf-exterior-power]. For a smooth model $M$ of $G$ with nonempty irreducible special fibre and generic point $\zeta$ of that fibre, write $n(M)=\operatorname{ord}_{\zeta}(\omega)$: this is the integer $n$ for which $\pi^{-n}\omega$ generates $\Omega^d_{M/R,\zeta}$. Suppose $G(E^{\mathrm{sh}})$ is bounded. The set of integers $n(M)$, for all smooth models $M$ with nonempty irreducible special fibre, has a minimum $n_0$. Call $M$ minimal when $n(M)=n_0$, and call two such models equivalent if the identity on $G$ extends to a $T$-birational map between them. There are finitely many equivalence classes, and at least one. Choose representatives $M_1,\ldots,M_r$. For every smooth finite-type $T$-scheme $Z$, every generic point $\xi$ of $Z_k$, and $A=\mathcal O_{Z,\xi}$ with fraction field $L$, the ring $A$ is a discrete valuation ring with uniformizer $\pi$. The minimum order for smooth $A$-models of $G_L$, measured using $\omega_L$ and $\pi$, is again $n_0$. The opens of $M_i\times_R A$ consisting of the entire generic fibre and one irreducible component of its special fibre are minimal $A$-models, and together represent all equivalence classes of minimal $A$-models (repetitions are permitted). The same conclusion holds if each $M_i$ is first shrunk by removing a closed subset contained in its special fibre and nowhere dense in that fibre.

proof.text: The identity of $G$ gives an $E^{\mathrm{sh}}$-point, so the bounded nonempty case of the weak-family lemma applies. Choose a finite nonempty weak Néron family $(N_j)_{j\in J}$ and refine it as that lemma permits, so every $(N_j)_k$ is nonempty and irreducible. The differential-order lemma makes $n_j=n(N_j)$ well-defined integers and supplies strict-henselian sections. Put $b=\min_{j\in J}n_j$; this minimum is attained because $J$ is finite nonempty.

source.place: 4.3 Proposition 2(i), first three sentences of proof; 3.5 Theorem 2 and component refinement

proof.text: Let $M$ be any smooth model of $G$ with nonempty irreducible special fibre. Apply the weak rational mapping property to the generic identity $M_E\simeq G$: it extends to a trait-rational map $M\dashrightarrow N_j$ for some $j$. Its multiplier on $\omega$ is $a=1$, of valuation zero on a strict-henselian section supplied by the differential-order lemma. That lemma yields $n(M)\geq n_j\geq b$. Some $N_j$ has order $b$, so the minimum in the question exists and $n_0=b$.

source.place: 4.3 Proposition 2(i), weak-rational-map argument and application of Lemma 1(i)

proof.text: If $M$ is minimal, the inequalities in Step 2 force $n_j=n_0$. The equal-order clause of the differential-order lemma says that $M\dashrightarrow N_j$ is an open immersion on its domain. That domain is dense in both fibres, and its image meets $(N_j)_k$; since the latter is irreducible, this open image is dense there, and the generic identity has dense image in the generic fibre. Thus $M$ and $N_j$ are equivalent. Every minimal class therefore contains one of the finitely many $N_j$ with $n_j=n_0$. There is at least one such $j$. This proves finiteness and nonemptiness of the classes; fix any set $(M_i)_{1\leq i\leq r}$ of representatives.

Fix $Z,\xi,A,L$ as in the statement. The weak-family lemma gives that $A$ is a DVR with uniformizer $\pi$, and that $(N_j\times_R A)$ is a weak Néron family of $G_L$. Refine this family into opens with entire generic fibre and one nonempty irreducible special component, using the same lemma over $A$. For any original smooth model $P$ with irreducible special fibre, and any component $C$ of $(P_A)_{\kappa(\xi)}$, its generic point $\eta'$ maps to the generic point $\eta$ of $P_k$: the field-extension projection is open by the universally-open lemma, and $C$ is an open component as in the permitted smooth-fibre refinement. Hence its image is a nonempty open of the irreducible $P_k$. Continuity gives $p(C)\subseteq\overline{\{p(\eta')\}}$, so $p(\eta')=\eta$. This applies to both $P=N_j$ and $P=M_i$.

source.place: 4.3 Lemma 3, first two sentences of proof; 3.5 Corollary 4 and Stacks Tag 0383

proof.text: For $P,C,\eta,\eta'$ in Step 4, set $n=n(P)$. In the line $\Omega^d_{P/R,\eta}$ the element $\lambda=\pi^{-n}\omega$ is a basis by the definition of order. The affine differential base-change isomorphism, followed by localization at these points, identifies the relative differentials after $R\to A$ with the tensor extension of the original differentials. Taking $d$th exterior powers gives the same identification for the top lines: on pure wedges its map is $(a_1\otimes e_1)\wedge\cdots\wedge(a_d\otimes e_d)\mapsto(a_1\cdots a_d)\otimes(e_1\wedge\cdots\wedge e_d)$, with inverse $a\otimes(e_1\wedge\cdots\wedge e_d)\mapsto(a\otimes e_1)\wedge(1\otimes e_2)\wedge\cdots\wedge(1\otimes e_d)$. These inverse maps descend by multilinearity and the alternating relations; in degree zero both are the scalar identification. Thus $1\otimes\lambda=\pi^{-n}\omega_L$ is a basis at $\eta'$. The same $\pi$ is a uniformizer at that special generic point by the differential-order lemma over $A$. Consequently the component open of $P_A$ has order exactly $n(P)$.

source.place: 4.3 Lemma 3, equality of orders; Stacks Tag 00RV and the defining alternating relations for exterior powers

proof.text: Write $N_{j,\alpha}$ for the component opens of the base-changed weak family. Step 5 gives $n(N_{j,\alpha})=n_j$. Each $N_j$ has a nonempty special fibre after extending the residue field, so every $j$ contributes a component. The minimum of these orders is therefore $n_0$. Repeat Step 2 over the DVR $A$, using this weak family and the pulled-back invariant form: every smooth $A$-model with nonempty irreducible special fibre maps rationally, by the generic identity, to some $N_{j,\alpha}$; the multiplier is $1$, with valuation zero on a section. Order comparison bounds its order below by $n_j\geq n_0$. A component with $n_j=n_0$ attains the bound. Thus the minimum over $A$ is precisely $n_0$, and the equal-order argument of Step 3 shows that every minimal $A$-model is equivalent to an $N_{j,\alpha}$ with $n_j=n_0$.

source.place: 4.3 Lemma 3, completion of the weak-family and order-comparison argument

proof.text: For each $j$ with $n_j=n_0$, choose $i$ such that $N_j$ is equivalent to $M_i$ over $R$. The base-change clause of the rational-spreading lemma takes the witnessing birational identity to a birational identity over $A$. Its two dense opens meet every special component. An isomorphism between them matches each special component on the $N_j$ side with one on the $M_i$ side. Restricting to that matched pair gives a birational identity between their component opens (adjoining the entire generic fibre on both sides, where the map is already the identity). Step 5 gives order $n_0$ for every component open of every $M_i\times_R A$. These opens are therefore minimal by Step 6, and Step 6 and these restricted birational identities show that they cover all minimal classes over $A$. Different components or representatives may give the same class, as allowed.

source.place: 4.3 Lemma 3, passage from a weak family to any chosen minimal representatives

proof.text: For the final clause let $H_i\subseteq(M_i)_k$ be closed and nowhere dense, and replace $M_i$ by $M_i\setminus H_i$. This open contains the entire generic fibre and the special generic point, so its order is still $n_0$ and its inclusion is a birational identity. After $R\to A$ it remains dense in each fibre by the density clause of the rational-spreading lemma. It therefore meets every special component densely; its component opens have the same local rings at their special generic points as the unshrunk ones. They have order $n_0$ and the same birational classes. Hence all the conclusions of Step 7 persist after the stated shrinking.
